title: Paul's journeys
hook: many miles on foot and by sea, making tents to pay his way

segments.voice: Yesterday, the council of Jerusalem, and your line was it seemed good to the spirit and us. What did you set down that wasn't necessary? Now the road is open. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
screen: `IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT AND US.`

segments.voice: A workshop in Corinth. Needles, heavy thread, a length of rough material pinned across a bench, and three people working it: a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, and a traveler who has just arrived from Athens. Acts says it simply: "because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." The traveler is Paul. His road fills the later chapters of Acts. And on a weekday in Corinth he is sewing tents to pay his way. Today is about the roads he walked, and the work he did with his hands along the way.

Acts follows Paul out of Antioch, with Barnabas, across the sea to Cyprus and up into the hill towns of Asia Minor. Later, in Troas on the coast, he sees a man in the night, in a vision, saying: "Come over into Macedonia, and help us." So he crosses into Europe. In Philippi a businesswoman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, opens her home to the new church. Then Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus. Acts never numbers his trips. Readers draw them as journeys on maps in the back of their Bibles, but Acts tells it as one long road. And the road was hard. Paul lists it himself, in a letter to Corinth: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers." Then, the tents. Why work at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians: "labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you." He didn't want the message to come with a bill. To the elders of Ephesus he holds up his own hands: "these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me." Not only his own needs. His friends' too. So the picture of Paul isn't just the preacher in the marketplace. It's the man at the bench with a needle in his hand, who also "reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath." Some Christians who work ordinary jobs while serving a church call themselves tentmakers, after him.

Here's the practice: walk Paul's road on a map. If you have a phone or an atlas handy, find the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea. Look for Antioch in the corner where Turkey meets Syria, then Cyprus, then Philippi in northern Greece, then Athens and Corinth to the south, then Ephesus across the water. Trace the line slowly with a finger. If you can't look at a map right now, close your eyes and walk it in your mind: a coast, a ship, a dusty road, a workshop. If you pray, you can pray for someone traveling today. The bell holds the time.
Paul's journeys. The roads and sea crossings Acts follows, from Antioch to Europe and back, paid for by a tentmaker's hands.

Your line: he made tents. This week the twelve went everywhere, a council kept the door open, and Paul walked through it. Today, do your ordinary work as part of something bigger. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read Paul's journeys in Acts and in his letters, often with the maps printed in the back of some Bibles, and people who serve a church while working an ordinary job are sometimes called tentmakers after him.

myth: Acts numbers Paul's journeys one, two and three
Acts tells one long road. readers number the journeys on maps.
Paul worked as a tentmaker while he preached
Acts 18:3: "by their occupation they were tentmakers."

fork.setup: you're Paul in Corinth. you could ask the church to support you and preach full-time. what do you do?
options: accept the support; preaching is your job.
work a trade with your own hands so you aren't a burden.
move on to a richer city.
fork.reveal: he makes tents with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3). he told the Thessalonians why: "because we would not be chargeable unto any of you."

what it means: he walked and sailed a long road, and paid his own way sewing tents.
what a scholar hears: Acts never numbers the journeys; the numbered routes on Bible maps come from later readers.

notes: Editor pass: invented 'preached in the evenings' replaced with Acts 18:4 (KJV); 'second half of Acts' softened; tentmaker label limited to 'some Christians'; fork no longer claims the church offered support; trapdoor's claim about the writer's interests cut.

'The missionary whose road fills the second half of Acts': Acts 13–28 follow Paul. Confirm.
The tentmaking scene's materials (needles, heavy thread, rough material) are deliberately generic; the material of ancient tents (leather or goat-hair cloth) is debated.
'Christians who work ordinary jobs while serving a church still call themselves tentmakers, after him': the modern term 'tentmaking ministry'. Confirm.
Map directions in the practice (Antioch near the Turkey–Syria border; Philippi in northern Greece) are geography, not text claims; confirm.
